plan.topic: Is there a plague vaccine? The live EV vaccine given to at-risk workers in former Soviet countries since the 1930s, vs no licensed plague vaccine for the general public in the US
plan.angle: 35–50 s. Open: 'Is there a plague vaccine? In the US, CDC says no plague vaccine is available. Antibiotics and public-health measures are the main tools.' Then: 'Russia and some neighbouring countries use a live vaccine called EV, in use since the mid-1930s, mainly for people at high risk such as lab staff working with live plague cultures. It can cause strong reactions, and CDC says there isn't strong evidence that older vaccines protect against the pneumonic form.' No mention of the Irkutsk worker's vaccination. Close: 'Early antibiotics save lives. With possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Title: 'Is There a Plague Vaccine? The US vs Russia #shorts'.
plan.working_title: Is There a Plague Vaccine? What Lab Workers Get #shorts
plan.why: Contrarian-but-true slot. 'She was vaccinated' raises an obvious question almost no outlet has explained. Low competition, with a peer-reviewed review to build on. | fact-check: (1) CDC's wording is 'A plague vaccine is not available' in the US. Don't narrow it to 'for the general public', which suggests some people in the US can get one. CDC also says there isn't strong evidence that vaccines used elsewhere protect against pneumonic plague; keep that line. (2) EV: PMC reviews confirm the live EV NIIEG vaccine has been used since the mid-1930s in the former USSR and is still used in Russia and Kazakhstan. They also note it causes strong reactions and that use outside Russia has declined (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4317636/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6559729/). (3) Drop the line about the Irkutsk worker's vaccination. I couldn't find it in Euronews (its Oct 4 article doesn't mention it). Plague isn't confirmed in her case, so the line would suggest a vaccine failure that hasn't been shown, and it puts the person who died at the centre. (4) The title 'What Lab Workers Get' suggests US lab workers get a vaccine. Change it.

Russia and Kazakhstan use a live vaccine called EV, mainly for people in high-risk jobs. WHO doesn't recommend plague vaccination except for high-risk groups, like lab staff and health workers. script.hook_pattern: The script asks a plain search question out loud and puts it on the first frame. It answers within 5 seconds with CDC's own wording: a plague vaccine is no longer available in the US. The twist is that some countries still vaccinate high-risk groups. The catch is credited to the review that actually says it, and the two reviews' disagreement on side effects is stated openly. The ending loops back to the opening question.

factcheck.summary:
I checked all 6 sources and they exist. Most claims match them word for word:
- CDC says "A plague vaccine is no longer available in the United States" (last reviewed Mar 5, 2025).
- CDC says plague "can be cured with antibiotics, but these must be given promptly" (last reviewed Aug 24, 2026).
- WHO's fact sheet (29 Sep 2026) says WHO doesn't recommend vaccination except for high-risk groups such as lab staff and health workers.
- Feodorova 2014 says the live EV vaccine has been used "since the mid-1930s".
- Sun 2016 says it is "still used and commercially available in Russia and Kazakhstan".
- The two reviews really do disagree on side effects: Feodorova calls reactions "generally mild", while Sun says the live vaccines were "rarely used outside of Russia due to their strong adverse reactions".
- CDC's 4 pneumonic warning signs are given in full, with the urgent-care line.

One major error, in s4: "Some vaccinated people still caught it" comes from a Sun 2016 sentence about the killed whole-cell USP vaccine, not the live EV vaccine. Neither review reports breakthrough cases after EV, so the line moves a finding from one vaccine to another. s4 also says "one review" found EV less reliable against pneumonic plague, but both reviews say it protects "to some extent", so this isn't a point where they disagree. There are also two small scope fixes in s3 and s1. Safety framing is good: no self-treatment and no fear-bait.

issues.claim: Some vaccinated people still caught it.
issues.problem: This is about the wrong vaccine. Sun 2016 says "several humans contracted pneumonic plague despite immunization with this vaccine", but that sentence is about the killed whole-cell (USP) vaccine, not the live EV vaccine this scene covers. Neither review reports EV breakthrough cases. Feodorova 2014 reports no recorded vaccine-related deaths or serious complications, and says nothing about breakthrough cases.
issues.fix: Here's the catch: reviews disagree on how harsh its side effects are. And both reviews say it protects against pneumonic plague, the form that can spread between people, only to some extent.

issues.claim: One review: live vaccine less reliable against pneumonic plague; attribution Sun 2016
issues.problem: Both Feodorova 2014 and Sun 2016 say the vaccine works against bubonic and "to some extent, pneumonic plague". Saying "one review" suggests the other review disagrees, which it doesn't.
issues.fix: fact: "Reviews: live vaccine protects against pneumonic plague only to some extent"; attribution: "Peer-reviewed reviews (Feodorova 2014; Sun 2016, PMC)"

issues.claim: mainly for people in high-risk jobs
issues.problem: Too narrow. Feodorova 2014 says people at occupational risk and residents of plague-endemic areas are both vaccinated.
issues.fix: Russia and Kazakhstan use a live vaccine called EV, in use since the mid-1930s, mainly for people in high-risk jobs and in plague areas. WHO doesn't recommend plague vaccination except for high-risk groups, like lab staff and health workers.

issues.problem: "None" could read as if a vaccine never existed or none is being developed. CDC says one is "no longer available" and new ones are in development.

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: The fact-checker's major error hasn't been fixed. "Some vaccinated people still caught it" comes from Sun 2016's passage on the killed USP vaccine, but the piece applies it to the live EV vaccine, and the Instagram caption still repeats it. The "one review" framing on pneumonic protection is also still in the Instagram and Facebook captions, even though both reviews say EV protects only "to some extent", so viewers would get a false picture of EV's track record.

audio.soundNotes: Trimmed two overcrowded SFX clusters (the 0–0.6s open and the 7.5–8.1s label-pop) down to 3–4 events each by dropping duplicate/layered sounds, and pulled down two cues (i3, i56) that were sitting 2–3 dB louder than the −14 to −20 dB speech target. Music is left essentially flat (×1.15, ~+1.2 dB): under-voice measured at −13.5 dB is already inside the −12/−15 target, so a bigger boost isn't safe even though pauses measured too quiet at −19.8 dB — a single overall multiplier can't fix the pause level without overshooting the under-speech ceiling, so that gap needs fixing on the ducking/pause-boost side, not here. Added five bespoke cues (history whir for the 1930s stat, a tense pivot stab for "here's the catch", a soft breath for the pneumonic/lungs label, and a warm resolving chime for the closing line) to give key story beats a distinct identity without competing with narration.

issues.claim: WHO only recommends plague vaccination for high-risk groups, not the general public.
issues.problem: 'Only recommends' makes it sound as if WHO actively recommends the vaccine for high-risk groups. The verified script, like WHO, says the opposite way round: vaccination is not recommended except for high-risk groups. 'Not the general public' also adds our own inference.
issues.fix: WHO doesn't recommend plague vaccination except for high-risk groups, like lab staff and health workers.

issues.claim: Russia and Kazakhstan still use a live vaccine called EV, in use since the mid-1930s, mainly for people in high-risk jobs like lab staff. / ...like lab workers.
issues.problem: In the verified script, 'lab staff and health workers' are WHO's examples of high-risk groups. They are not the stated users of EV in Russia and Kazakhstan. Attaching them to the EV sentence mixes up the two sources.
issues.fix: Instagram: "Russia and Kazakhstan still use a live vaccine called EV, in use since the mid-1930s, mainly for people in high-risk jobs." Facebook: "But Russia and Kazakhstan still use a live vaccine called EV, in use since the mid-1930s, mainly for people in high-risk jobs."

issues.claim: one review found it's less reliable against pneumonic plague
issues.problem: The verified script says the review 'says' this. 'Found' makes it sound like a new study result. This is wording polish only.
issues.fix: Reviews disagree on how harsh its side effects are, and one review says it's less reliable against pneumonic plague — the form that can spread between people. Some vaccinated people still caught it.
